idiom_name: module mixin with the included hook plus blocks/procs; ViewComponent/Stimulus in Rails
implementation_notes: Ruby packages reusable behaviour in modules and blocks: the Module documentation defines a module as a collection of methods whose instance methods appear in a class when the module is included, so stateful behaviour is mixed in with include/extend and a self.included hook wires per-host setup at inclusion time - no wrapper object or base class per consumer. Blocks and procs are the callback surface, instance variables inside the mixin hold per-host state, and Module.new with a block allows modules to be built programmatically. In Rails UI code the same reuse is served by ViewComponent classes and Stimulus controllers rather than by component wrappers; keep a plain class or service object when the behaviour needs its own lifecycle instead of participating in a host.
code_sketch:
module Subscribable
  def self.included(base)
    base.attr_reader :subscriptions
  end

  def subscribe(target, event, &block)
    (@subscriptions ||= []) << [target, event, block]
    target.add_listener(event, block)
  end

  def unsubscribe_all
    (@subscriptions || []).each { |t, e, b| t.remove_listener(e, b) }
    @subscriptions = []
  end
end

class Widget
  include Subscribable
end
pitfalls: Module methods share the host's instance variables: two modules using the same variable name collide, and mixin order decides which method implementation wins.
Blocks capture their defining binding, so a long-lived subscription keeps that scope (and any stale references in it) alive; use explicit objects for long-lived callbacks.
Including stateful behaviour into view objects recreates controller logic in the view layer; ViewComponent and Stimulus exist to keep that boundary intact.
